title: Multi-Agent Guided Policy Optimization
one_liner: A framework that trains all agents together as one to guide how each agent acts alone.
lead: In the real world, robots and agents often cannot talk to each other or see what the others see. Yet they must work together. MAGPO solves this by training them all at once in a classroom (seeing everything), then deploying each one into the field (seeing only its own view). The trick: teach them how to coordinate during training, then give each agent a compass that steers it toward coordinated behavior even when flying solo.

problem.h2: Why teams of agents struggle in the real world
paras: A naive approach: train each agent to maximize its own reward (its personal goal). But when agents collide or share space, selfish behavior causes chaos. A team of delivery drones each trying to reach a destination first will crash into one another.

A smarter approach: train all agents together, sharing information about everyone's position and plan. This works perfectly in simulation. Deploy it to the real world, and it breaks: the agents cannot actually see each other, cannot hear each other, and cannot stay connected to a central brain. The trained policy assumes data that will never arrive.

callout.html: Training assumes a god's-eye view (all agents visible, all positions known). Deployment requires each agent to act alone with only a partial, local view.

panels.title: 1. The naive dream
panels.caption: Each drone wants only its own reward. Chaos and collisions result.

panels.title: 2. The classroom solution
panels.viz_args: Central brain sees all. All drones fed full state.
panels.caption: In training, a central authority sees everything and coordinates perfectly.

panels.title: 3. The deployment shock
panels.caption: Deploy: each drone flies blind with only its own sensors. Coordination vanishes.

panels.title: 4. MAGPO's compass
panels.caption: Each agent learns a shared compass from central training. Drones now pull toward coordination.

panels.title: 5. Coordinated flight
panels.caption: Each drone acts alone but steers itself toward the team's goals learned together.

steps.text: Build one super-policy that sees all agents and their states at once. It learns perfect coordination.
Distill what the oracle learned into a signal that one agent can use: a shared alignment target (a reference policy all agents want to match).
Each agent trains alone, seeing only its own sensors, but also trains to stay close to the shared target learned in step 1.
Explicitly measure how close each agent's behavior is to the target. Steer it back if it drifts.
Each agent carries the alignment target. With no central brain in the loop, it acts to match the target and coordinate with teammates implicitly.

paras: The paper modifies how agents learn: it adds a shared alignment target (a reference policy learned during centralized training) that each decentralized agent tries to follow during execution.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: policy alignment gap
hidden.name: How far each agent drifts from coordination
paras: During decentralized training, each agent learns a policy (a rule for what to do in any situation). The problem: that policy can stray far from what the central oracle learned. MAGPO measures this drift—the difference between the decentralized policy and the shared target. Call it the alignment gap.

The paper estimates this gap by comparing each agent's actions to the reference policy under identical starting states. A large gap means the agent has learned to ignore the central guidance. MAGPO uses this gap as a loss signal: the training nudges each agent to shrink the gap, keeping it tethered to coordination.

heat.caption: Darker means larger drift from the shared target. MAGPO penalizes large drift (marked cells).

reads.html: Alignment gap is the mismatch between what an agent learned and what the team learned together.

The paper uses divergence-based metrics (e.g. KL divergence, a way to measure how different two probability distributions are — think of them as likelihood profiles for different actions). These metrics compare the decentralized policy to the reference policy to quantify the gap.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: steering without a leash
paras: Here is the causal chain: In the classroom (centralized training), a single policy learns coordination. This policy is built one action at a time—autoregressive (each agent picks its move in sequence, seeing what earlier agents chose). This sequential action gives the oracle the full picture to make each agent's move reinforce the team's goals.

That oracle becomes the compass. When you deploy an individual agent into the wild, it cannot call home. Instead, it carries a copy of the compass: an internal goal to match the oracle's behavior under similar conditions. When the agent faces a choice (turn left or right), it picks the option closest to what the oracle would pick. This is alignment loss: a penalty that grows when the agent strays.

The genius move: the alignment loss is computed during training only (not deployment). So agents learn early and often to stay in sync. By the time they go live, staying aligned feels natural—the agent's own learned behavior already matches the shared target. No central nudging is needed.

stages.s: Autoregressive oracle picks one agent's action, sees result
Extract alignment target from oracle's sequence
Train each agent to match the target while maximizing its own reward
Deployment: each agent uses learned policy plus remembered alignment

math.words: total loss = (negative reward for the task) plus (lambda times the average alignment gap across all agents)
symbols: the team reward for the current task
how strongly to penalize drifting from alignment
the policy learned by agent i acting alone
the oracle's policy focused on agent i's decisions
a measure of how different two probability distributions are (larger = more different)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose Agent 1 has alignment gap D_KL = 0.3 (a mild drift), Agent 2 has gap 0.1 (tight alignment), Agent 3 has gap 0.7 (severe drift).
The loss improved (less negative is better when training nudges the weights downhill), rewarding the team for tighter alignment.

math.note: The equation pulls agents toward both doing well (maximizing R) and staying aligned (minimizing the sum of drifts).

charts.title: Naive decentralized training
charts.note: Without guidance, agents learn to ignore each other and fail at the team goal.

charts.title: MAGPO with central guidance
charts.note: Alignment loss keeps agents tethered to coordinated behavior learned during centralized training.

items.html: If lambda (the alignment weight) is too high, agents become slaves to the oracle and forget to adapt to their own local observations. They match the target perfectly but fail when they encounter situations the oracle never trained on.
If lambda is too low, agents ignore alignment and fall back to selfish behavior. They wander far from coordination.

items.b: Oracle sees data deployment will not see.
items.html: If the central oracle trains on observations (e.g., other agents' exact positions) that the decentralized agents will never receive, the alignment target becomes unachievable, and the agent wastes effort chasing an impossible goal.

MAGPO works when lambda is tuned to the task (moderate penalty), the oracle is constrained to predict only from data each agent will have at deployment, and agents train long enough to internalize alignment.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple multi-agent coordination task: three agents in a 2D grid trying to reach goal positions without colliding, each seeing only a radius around itself. Train a central oracle that sees all three agents and picks a sequence of moves. Extract the alignment target (the oracle's policy compressed for one agent). Train three decentralized agents on the same task, adding the alignment loss. Measure: (a) how often agents reach their goals, (b) how many collisions occur, (c) the average KL divergence between each agent's learned policy and the oracle's target under the same observation.
demo.closing: The demo must show that alignment loss shrinks the KL divergence and raises coordination quality, even though agents train alone with partial observations.
